Interpretable and Validatable Uplift Modeling

Bob Wilson Affiliation: Marketing Data Science at Meta Work done at Meta
Abstract

Uplift models estimate treatment effects for individuals, but we do not observe individual treatment effects, so the predictions are hard to interpret and validate. A decision-maker often wants trustworthy claims about groups where the treatment is beneficial or harmful, and to know when a treatment benefits some people more than others. Our procedure provides such a set of claims, certified simultaneously at a specified familywise error rate (FWER). We summarize an uplift model by a shallow tree fit to its predictions. Each node of the tree carries two hypotheses, one about the average treatment effect in the node and one about the difference in effects across the node’s split; the two kinds are interwoven into a single hierarchy. Splitting the data enables honest estimation in the evaluation set. It lets us choose the direction of each one-sided test from the training half, allowing us to certify the sign of treatment effects in subpopulations, and to compare effects between groups. We demonstrate our procedure offers strong control of the FWER.

††date: October 2026††correspondence: Bob Wilson at rwilson4@meta.com

1 Introduction

Uplift modeling uses observed covariates, XX, to estimate the impact of a treatment on each individual person:

τ⁡(x):=𝐄⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)|X=x],\tau(x):=\mathbf{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\,|\,X=x],

where (Y⁡(0),Y⁡(1)CLOSE(Y(0),Y(1) are potential outcomes. Gutierrez and Gérardy (2017) offer an introduction to the vast literature on uplift modeling.

Since individual treatment effects are unobservable, it can be difficult to validate an uplift model. Many researchers use random forests (Wager and Athey, 2018) or boosted trees (Powers et al., 2018) as model families, which are hard to interpret.

Previous work uses Qini or lift curves to summarize how well the model orders individuals by effect. The GATES of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) report average effects within quantile bins of the predicted score. The RATE of Yadlowsky et al. (2025) condenses targeting value into a single statistic with a confidence interval. These methods do not deliver insights about how the treatment performs in meaningful subpopulations. It is valuable to be able to say things like, the treatment benefits men more so than women, but overall it is beneficial for both groups, and to attach some claim of evidentiary strength.

Our method allows researchers to generate such claims, and to certify them as statistically significant. We split the data into training and evaluation sets. We fit the uplift model on the training set, then summarize it with a shallow regression tree. Turning to the evaluation set, we attach to each node two hypotheses: one about the average effect in the node, one about the difference in effects across the node’s split. We interweave the two kinds into a single hierarchy tested by a procedure controlling the familywise error rate, producing a set of trustworthy claims about meaningful subpopulations. More than reporting a single average treatment effect for the entire study population, our method offers rich insights about how treatment effects vary across the population, providing greater confidence or suitable caution to the decision maker.

The procedure rests on four components. The first splits the data to facilitate honest estimation. The second interweaves effect and heterogeneity hypotheses (§3), which lets the procedure consider treatment effects within subpopulations and differences in treatment effects across subpopulations. The third adapts the direction of each test to the training half of the data (§4): one-sided tests certify the treatment as beneficial or harmful in particular sub-groups, and more beneficial in some groups than others. The fourth sets the levels of individual tests to guarantee strong control of the FWER. None of these contributions are novel individually, but we have not seen them applied in combination in the context of uplift modeling.

§2 sets up the tree summary and the data split. §3 defines the hypotheses and their interweaving. §4 covers adaptive direction selection. §5 handles multiplicity. §6 offers a confidence bound as a consolation prize when we fail to reject a hypothesis. §7 presents the simulation study, and §8 concludes.

2 Interpretable Uplift Modeling

Researchers often use shallow decision trees to aid interpretability of otherwise inscrutable models, including for uplift modeling. The Virtual Twins procedure of Foster et al. (2011) fits a tree to individual effect estimates from a random forest. The aggregation trees of Di Francesco (2026) build a nested sequence of subgroups from estimated conditional effects. Wu et al. (2022) distill personalized experimentation results for interpretability at scale. Huang et al. (2025) pursue stable subgroup estimates from modern effect learners.

The resulting insights are informal and exploratory, reflecting a division of labor in the clinical trials literature. In their systematic review of subgroup methods, Ondra et al. (2016) separate confirmatory subgroup analysis, which considers a small number of prospectively defined subgroups and protects the familywise error rate across them, from exploratory analysis, which ranges over many candidate subgroups and where error rate control is typically not addressed at all. Prior work has treated uplift models as exploratory, searching a large space of subgroups and offering only suggestive rather than definitive conclusions. Our procedure goes a step farther, drawing rigorous conclusions from an exploratory search.

Although individual treatment effects are unobservable, random assignment identifies average treatment effects in a fixed population. The nodes of a decision tree are not fixed populations, because the selected nodes are a function of the data. The data-splitting method of Cox (1975) offers a solution: we divide the dataset into a training and an evaluation set, fit models (uplift and decision tree) on the training set, and draw conclusions from the evaluation set. Athey and Imbens (2016) use this strategy to derive unbiased estimates of treatment effects, a procedure they call honest estimation.

Their procedure emphasizes estimation rather than significance testing, and does not offer simultaneous control of error rates. Testing requires data splitting to make the subpopulations legitimate targets of inference, but we also need the multiplicity adjustment of §5 to make the resulting set of claims simultaneously credible. We control the familywise error rate (FWER), the probability of making at least one false statement, rather than the false discovery rate (FDR), the fraction of statements made which are false. While the FDR is valuable for exploratory work, it is a lower standard of evidence than the FWER and is thus unsuitable for confirmatory analysis: “any desired conclusion can be almost surely inferred without inflating the FDR” (Dmitrienko et al., 2009, page 39); see also Finner and Roters (2001).

3 Interweaving Hypotheses of Effect and Heterogeneity

Each node of the decision tree, SS, denotes a subpopulation. Each internal node has a split separating SS into children LL and R.R. We consider two kinds of hypotheses.

Effect.

What can we infer about the average treatment effect in SS? We consider one-sided hypotheses:

ES+:τS≤δSorES−:τS≥δS,E^{+}_{S}:\tau_{S}\leq\delta_{S}\qquad\text{or}\qquad E^{-}_{S}:\tau_{S}\geq\delta_{S},

where τS\tau_{S} is the average treatment effect in S,S, and δS\delta_{S} is a meaningful threshold we discuss below. Rejecting ES+E^{+}_{S} certifies—in the Frequentist sense of “certify” (Rubin, 2004)—the average treatment effect in SS is greater than δS\delta_{S}. Rejecting ES−E^{-}_{S} certifies the other direction, which is often just as valuable to know. §4 describes how we select the direction.

Setting δS=0\delta_{S}=0 allows us to identify the sign of the average treatment effect in a group. A small negative δi\delta_{i} implements a non-inferiority test, useful when ruling out catastrophic harm is more important than proving a benefit. When applying the treatment requires some resource, setting a suitable positive δi\delta_{i} can determine whether the benefit justifies the resource.

Heterogeneity.

Do the two subpopulations split at SS respond differently to treatment? Here also we consider one-sided hypotheses:

HSR:τR≤τLorHSL:τR≥τL.H^{R}_{S}:\tau_{R}\leq\tau_{L}\qquad\text{or}\qquad H^{L}_{S}:\tau_{R}\geq\tau_{L}.

As with the effect hypotheses, §4 discusses how to decide which to test. Rejecting HSRH^{R}_{S} certifies heterogeneity at the split and that the right child responds more positively.

We interweave the two families into a single hierarchy to support joint testing of both kinds of hypotheses. Each effect hypothesis has one child, the heterogeneity hypothesis at the same node. Each heterogeneity hypothesis has the effect hypotheses of the two child nodes as its children, as depicted in Figure 1. Leaves carry an effect hypothesis and no heterogeneity hypothesis, having no split beneath them.

4 Adaptively Selecting Hypotheses

Splitting the data does more than license inference after training. It also lets us adapt the hypotheses to the data. We only learn something when we reject a null hypothesis, so the goal is to reject as many hypotheses as possible, and for the corresponding alternatives to be informative.

We avoided two-sided hypotheses in the last section because the alternative is not informative. Rejecting A:θ=0A:\theta=0 only proves θ≠0\theta\neq 0 but does not determine the sign of θ\theta. Rejecting B:θ≤0B:\theta\leq 0 is informative, certifying θ>0\theta>0. A compelling strategy for two-sided testing tests both one-sided possibilities at half the level (as a Bonferroni adjustment), which does identify on which side the truth lies. But when we can anticipate the direction, we get more power by skipping one of these tests and allocating the full level to the one side.

In addition to providing the uplift model and the decision tree, the training set supports just this, suggesting a hypothesis to test at each node, ES+E_{S}^{+} or ES−E_{S}^{-}, and HSRH_{S}^{R} or HSLH_{S}^{L}. Write τ^S,train\hat{\tau}_{S,\textrm{train}} for the average treatment effect estimated in SS on the training set. If τ^S,train>δS\hat{\tau}_{S,\textrm{train}}>\delta_{S} we select ES+E_{S}^{+} to test on the evaluation set; otherwise we select ES−.E_{S}^{-}. Similarly, if τ^R,train>τ^L,train\hat{\tau}_{R,\textrm{train}}>\hat{\tau}_{L,\textrm{train}}, we select HSRH_{S}^{R} to test; otherwise, HSLH_{S}^{L}. Rejecting the selected hypotheses certifies what we observed informally in the training set.

Using one half of a sample to choose what to test and the other to test it is not new. Wasserman and Roeder (2009) screen variables on one half and clean up on the other, and Rubin et al. (2006) use a split to set cutoffs for a multiple testing procedure. Both select which hypotheses to test. Here we apply the method to uplift modeling.

5 Controlling the Familywise Error Rate

The methods proposed in this section operate on a finite or countable collection of hypotheses, Ai,i∈ℐ,A_{i},\,i\in\mathcal{I}, arranged in a tree-like hierarchy. The root node of this hierarchy will be called A1A_{1}. Each hypothesis ii has zero or more children indexed by 𝒥i.\mathcal{J}_{i}. Other than A1,A_{1}, all hypotheses have one parent hypothesis. In our case, A1A_{1} corresponds to the average treatment effect in the overall population.

Many existing techniques can take advantage of sequences or hierarchies of hypotheses to increase statistical power against certain alternatives. The Fixed Sequence Procedure (Maurer, 1995) and the Fallback Procedure (Wiens, 2003; Wiens and Dmitrienko, 2005) are two well-known examples. The intuition behind these procedures is “we pay only for our failures; successes are free”. When we test and reject a hypothesis, its level can be carried forward to later tests, increasing their power, but when we fail to reject a hypothesis, its level is “spent”.

Bretz et al. (2009) and Burman et al. (2009) developed graphical techniques generalizing the sequential procedures to hierarchies of hypotheses, and Goeman and Solari (2010) later identified the general principle. A graphical procedure is specified by an initial allocation aa of α\alpha across the hypotheses, with ∑iai≤α,\sum_{i}a_{i}\leq\alpha, and a transition matrix GG saying how a rejected hypothesis’s allocation is redistributed among the survivors. In §5.3, we discuss a special case of this strategy relevant to the hierarchy we propose.

5.1 Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure

This section gives a Bonferroni adjustment controlling the Familywise Error Rate, to measure the later methods against. Such an adjustment assigns a weight to each hypothesis. Provided the weights sum to no more than α\alpha, the adjustment controls the FWER at level α\alpha. Let nkn_{k} be the number of hypotheses at depth kk of the hierarchy, with the root node occurring at depth 1. For example, n1=1,n_{1}=1, n2=|𝒥1|,n_{2}=|\mathcal{J}_{1}|, where |𝒥1||\mathcal{J}_{1}| is the number of elements in 𝒥1\mathcal{J}_{1}, and n3=∑j∈𝒥1|𝒥j|.n_{3}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}|\mathcal{J}_{j}|.

The Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure tests A1A_{1} at level α/2.\alpha/2. It tests the hypotheses at depth kk at level 2−k⋅α/nk,2^{-k}\cdot\alpha/n_{k}, k=2,….k=2,\ldots. Since the levels at each depth sum to 2−k⋅α,2^{-k}\cdot\alpha, the sum of the levels across the entire hierarchy is ∑k2−k⋅α≤α.\sum_{k}2^{-k}\cdot\alpha\leq\alpha.

The Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure thus controls the FWER at the desired level, but the power corresponding to hypotheses lower in the hierarchy decreases exponentially. As a special case, consider a hierarchy where each hypothesis has two children. Then nk=2k−1,n_{k}=2^{k-1}, k=1,…,k=1,\ldots, and we test the hypotheses at depth kk at level 21−2⋅k⋅α.2^{1-2\cdot k}\cdot\alpha.

5.2 Fixed Hierarchy Procedure

As with the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure, we have a collection of hypotheses in a tree-like hierarchy. For this method, each hypothesis Ai,A_{i}, other than A1,A_{1}, has an associated weight, wi,w_{i}, with 0≤wi≤10\leq w_{i}\leq 1, and ∑j∈𝒥iwj=1\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}w_{j}=1 for all i.i.

The Fixed Hierarchy Procedure tests A1A_{1} at level α1=α.\alpha_{1}=\alpha. If we fail to reject A1A_{1} (henceforth we say “retain”), testing stops; otherwise, we test each child at level wj⋅α,w_{j}\cdot\alpha, j∈𝒥1.j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}. Progressing down the tree, if we test AiA_{i} at level αi,\alpha_{i}, and retain Ai,A_{i}, we do not test any descendants of AiA_{i}. Otherwise, we test each child of AiA_{i} at level wj⋅αi,w_{j}\cdot\alpha_{i}, j∈𝒥i.j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}.

Remark: the Fixed Sequence Procedure is a special case of the Fixed Hierarchy Procedure, where each hypothesis has at most one child.

This procedure is the hierarchical testing procedure of Meinshausen (2008), with the sibling weights generalized from proportional-to-size to arbitrary wj.w_{j}. It is the special case vi≡1v_{i}\equiv 1 of the procedure in §5.3. Strong control therefore follows from the argument in §5.3.

To compare the performance of the Fixed Hierarchy Procedure with the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure, consider a hierarchy where each hypothesis has two children, and wi=1/2w_{i}=1/2 for all ii. Assuming we reject all ancestors, the Fixed Hierarchy Procedure tests a hypothesis at depth kk at level 21−k⋅α,2^{1-k}\cdot\alpha, compared to 21−2⋅k⋅α2^{1-2\cdot k}\cdot\alpha for the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure. The Fixed Hierarchy Procedure can therefore be exponentially more powerful. It buys power with flexibility: retain the first hypothesis and it rejects nothing, including hypotheses the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure would have rejected. The method of the next section lets testing continue past a retention, at lower power.

One property of both Hierarchical Bonferroni and Fixed Hierarchy is that the level at which we test a hypothesis depends only on its depth. We may grow the tree another level without changing the level at which we test any existing hypothesis. Thus there is no reason to control the tree depth when constructing the tree on the training set. The power available to tests deep in the tree decreases exponentially, so at some point, we will retain all hypotheses below a certain depth. We may prune these nodes, leaving a shallower tree emphasizing the certified claims.

5.3 Trickle Down Procedure

As before, each hypothesis has a weight, wi.w_{i}. Each hypothesis now also has a stake, 0<vi≤1.0<v_{i}\leq 1. We mean the name in the sense of a wager: something risked. We also need the available level, which the stake converts into the level at which we test a hypothesis. If AiA_{i} has available level αi,\alpha_{i}, we test it at level vi⋅αi.v_{i}\cdot\alpha_{i}.

The Trickle Down Procedure assigns A1A_{1} to have available level α1:=α,\alpha_{1}:=\alpha, testing it at level v1⋅αv_{1}\cdot\alpha. The available level of hypotheses farther down in the hierarchy depends on which hypotheses farther up in the hierarchy we rejected. Suppose AiA_{i} has available level αi\alpha_{i} (and is thus tested at level vi⋅αiv_{i}\cdot\alpha_{i} ). We assign each child an available level depending on whether we rejected the parent:

αj:={wj⋅αiAi​ rejectedwj⋅(1−vi)⋅αiAi​ retained,\alpha_{j}:=\begin{cases}w_{j}\cdot\alpha_{i}&A_{i}\textrm{ rejected}\\ w_{j}\cdot(1-v_{i})\cdot\alpha_{i}&A_{i}\textrm{ retained},\end{cases}

j∈𝒥i.j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}.

When we test AiA_{i}, we wager only a portion, vi,v_{i}, of the available level, αi,\alpha_{i}, testing AiA_{i} at level vi⋅αiv_{i}\cdot\alpha_{i}. If we reject Ai,A_{i}, we split the entire available level, αi,\alpha_{i}, among the children. If we fail to reject Ai,A_{i}, the stake is forfeit, but the unwagered portion, (1−vi)⋅αi,(1-v_{i})\cdot\alpha_{i}, is still available for continued testing.

Remark: the Fixed Hierarchy Procedure is a special case of the Trickle Down Procedure, where vi=1v_{i}=1 for all i.i. The Fixed Hierarchy Procedure stakes the entire available level at each opportunity. The Fallback Procedure is analogous to the Trickle Down Procedure when each hypothesis has at most one child, but with different weights.

This procedure is an instance of the graphical approach of Bretz et al. (2009), developed independently and in parallel by Burman et al. (2009), and strong control of the familywise error rate follows from their results. The proof below is direct, and short enough to be worth giving in the notation of this paper.

We first record that the procedure is monotone in the available level.

Lemma 1.

Decreasing the available level at a node can only shrink the set of hypotheses rejected at or below it.

Proof.

Run the procedure from node ii twice, with available levels a≤a′.a\leq a^{\prime}. The node is tested at vi​av_{i}a and vi​a′,v_{i}a^{\prime}, so if it is rejected under aa it is rejected under a′.a^{\prime}. Each child then receives (1−vi)​wj​a(1-v_{i})w_{j}a or wj​aw_{j}a in the first run, according to whether AiA_{i} was retained or rejected, and the corresponding quantity with a′a^{\prime} in the second. In every case the child’s available level in the first run is no larger than in the second, because a≤a′a\leq a^{\prime} and 1−vi≤1.1-v_{i}\leq 1. Descending the subtree gives the claim. ∎

Proposition 1.

The probability the Trickle Down Procedure rejects at least one true hypothesis is at most α.\alpha.

Proof.

For a node ii and a level a>0,a>0, let Fi​(a)F_{i}(a) be the event that the procedure, run on the subtree rooted at ii with available level a,a, rejects at least one true hypothesis. Each such run is a function of the same pp-values, so these events are all defined on one probability space. We show Pr​{Fi​(a)}≤a\mathrm{Pr}\left\{F_{i}(a)\right\}\leq a by induction up from the leaves; the proposition is the case i=1,i=1, a=α.a=\alpha.

If ii is a leaf and AiA_{i} is false, Fi​(a)F_{i}(a) is empty. If AiA_{i} is true, Fi​(a)F_{i}(a) is the event that the test at ii rejects, which has probability at most vi​a≤a.v_{i}a\leq a.

Now let ii have children 𝒥i,\mathcal{J}_{i}, and suppose the claim holds for each child. Suppose first that AiA_{i} is true. Rejecting it is itself a false rejection, and when it is retained each child receives available level (1−vi)​wj​a,(1-v_{i})w_{j}a, so

Fi​(a)⊆{Ai​ rejected}∪⋃j∈𝒥iFj​((1−vi)​wj​a).F_{i}(a)\;\subseteq\;\left\{A_{i}\textrm{ rejected}\right\}\;\cup\;\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}F_{j}\bigl((1-v_{i})\,w_{j}\,a\bigr).

The union bound and the inductive hypothesis give

Pr⁡{Fi​(a)}≤vi​a+∑j∈𝒥i(1−vi)​wj​a=vi​a+(1−vi)​a=a.\mathrm{Pr}\left\{F_{i}(a)\right\}\;\leq\;v_{i}\,a+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}(1-v_{i})\,w_{j}\,a\;=\;v_{i}\,a+(1-v_{i})\,a\;=\;a.

Suppose instead that AiA_{i} is false. Rejecting it is not an error, and each child receives available level either wj​aw_{j}a or (1−vi)​wj​a,(1-v_{i})w_{j}a, both at most wj​a.w_{j}a. By Lemma 1,

Fi​(a)⊆⋃j∈𝒥iFj​(wj​a),F_{i}(a)\;\subseteq\;\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}F_{j}(w_{j}\,a),

so Pr⁡{Fi​(a)}≤∑j∈𝒥iwj​a=a.\mathrm{Pr}\left\{F_{i}(a)\right\}\leq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}w_{j}\,a=a. ∎

The Trickle Down Procedure is more flexible than the Fixed Hierarchy Procedure and can be more powerful than the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure. To see this, suppose each hypothesis has two children, and let wi=vi=1/2w_{i}=v_{i}=1/2 for all ii. The level at which we test hypotheses, other than the root hypothesis, depends on whether we reject earlier hypotheses.

Consider then two possibilities: first that we have rejected all hypotheses, second that we have retained all hypotheses. Table 1 shows the level at which we test a hypothesis at a particular depth. When we retain all hypotheses, the Trickle Down Procedure is no better (and no worse) than the Hierarchical Bonferroni Procedure. When we reject a hypothesis, we test later hypotheses at higher levels than with Hierarchical Bonferroni.

Remark 1.

One consequence of the tree parameterization is that it only exhausts α\alpha when all leaves have v=1v=1. Since Fixed Hierarchy sets v=1v=1 for all nodes, it is α\alpha-exhaustive.

6 Confidence Bounds for Retained Hypotheses

As we get deeper in the tree, available level decreases and we may retain some hypotheses. This section describes a consolation prize: a confidence bound corresponding to a weakened form of the hypothesis.

Let θ≥0\theta\geq 0. Let the weakened version of a hypothesis be as follows:

  • •

    ES+​(θ):τS≤δS−θE_{S}^{+}(\theta):\tau_{S}\leq\delta_{S}-\theta

  • •

    ES−​(θ):τS≥δS+θE_{S}^{-}(\theta):\tau_{S}\geq\delta_{S}+\theta

  • •

    HSR​(θ):τR≤τL−θH_{S}^{R}(\theta):\tau_{R}\leq\tau_{L}-\theta

  • •

    HSL​(θ):τR≥τL+θH_{S}^{L}(\theta):\tau_{R}\geq\tau_{L}+\theta

Weaker versions (having larger values of θ\theta) are easier to reject. At θ=0,\theta=0, the weakened version corresponds to the non-weakened version.

We may fail to reject a (non-weakened) hypothesis, but we can report the smallest θ\theta at which we can reject the weakened hypothesis. For example, when testing ES+E_{S}^{+} with δS=0\delta_{S}=0, we may not be able to prove the treatment is beneficial, but we can calculate a bound on how harmful it is.

Proposition 2.

Run the Trickle Down Procedure on the hierarchy of §3, and let each node report the smallest θ≥0\theta\geq 0 where the weakened hypothesis is rejected. The probability that any node falsely rejects a weakened hypothesis is still at most α.\alpha.

Proof.

Fix a node and write A⁡(θ)A(\theta) for the weakened hypotheses it tests. A⁡(0)A(0) is the hypothesis the Trickle Down Procedure tests. Let θ0\theta_{0} be the margin by which A⁡(0)A(0) holds: for example, δS−τS\delta_{S}-\tau_{S} for ES+​(θ).E^{+}_{S}(\theta). In each case A⁡(θ)A(\theta) is true if and only if θ≤θ0\theta\leq\theta_{0}. A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0}) is true, holding with equality. When θ0≥0\theta_{0}\geq 0, A⁡(0)A(0) is true. Because we consider only θ≥0\theta\geq 0, when θ0<0\theta_{0}<0, the node never considers a true hypothesis and can reject no true hypothesis, so assume θ0≥0\theta_{0}\geq 0.

The pp-value decreases in θ\theta, so the node rejects for θ≥θ⋆\theta\geq\theta^{\star}. If the node rejects A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0}) it has rejected a true hypothesis. Conversely, if the node rejects a true hypothesis, then A⁡(θ)A(\theta) is true for some θ≥θ⋆\theta\geq\theta^{\star}; any such θ\theta is at most θ0\theta_{0}, so θ⋆≤θ0\theta^{\star}\leq\theta_{0} and the node rejects A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0}). The event “the node rejects a true hypothesis” is therefore the event “the node rejects A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0})”.

We test all hypotheses A⁡(θ)A(\theta) for θ≥0\theta\geq 0, including A⁡(θ0),A(\theta_{0}), at the same level at which we test A⁡(0)A(0), so the probability of falsely rejecting A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0}) and the probability of falsely rejecting A⁡(0)A(0) are both at most that level.

The enlarged family therefore presents the procedure of §5.3 with the same hierarchy, the same weights and stakes, and one valid test at each node, which is all Proposition 1 requires. Only the statement each node makes has changed. ∎

Less formally: every way a node can be wrong about its bound is the same failure, rejecting A⁡(θ0)A(\theta_{0}), and our procedure controls the probability of a false rejection. Reporting the bound adds no new opportunity to be wrong. The restriction θ≥0\theta\geq 0 is necessary. We cannot compute a confidence bound corresponding to a rejected hypothesis without finding a threshold at which we retain the strengthened hypothesis, which prevents trickling its power down to later hypotheses. The asymmetry restates the principle: successes are free; failures are not.

7 Simulation Study

We investigated two aspects of the procedures: whether they control the familywise error rate (§7.2), and their ability to certify true effects (§7.3). We begin with a single worked run.

7.1 A worked example

We generated 10,000 individuals, each described by ten features: a continuous outcome predictor x0,x_{0}, a three-level categorical outcome predictor x1,x_{1}, two binary effect moderators x2x_{2} and x3,x_{3}, and six independent standard-normal noise variables x4,…,x9x_{4},\ldots,x_{9}. The baseline outcome was Y⁡(0)=x0+0.3​x1+ε0Y(0)=x_{0}+0.3x_{1}+\varepsilon_{0} with ε0∼𝒩⁡(0,9),\varepsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,9), and Y⁡(1)=Y⁡(0)+τ⁡(x)+ε1Y(1)=Y(0)+\tau(x)+\varepsilon_{1} with ε1\varepsilon_{1} independent of ε0.\varepsilon_{0}. The true treatment effect depended only on the two binary moderators:

We split the population evenly across the four moderator levels, so the population average treatment effect was +0.925+0.925. The average is misleading: the x2=0,x_{2}=0, x3=0x_{3}=0 subpopulation experienced a negative treatment effect masked by the others. The average treatment effect among people having x2=0x_{2}=0 is +0.1,+0.1, but the average conceals a strong positive effect just canceling out a strong negative effect. We assigned each individual to treatment or control with equal probability, recorded the corresponding potential outcome, and split the sample into training and evaluation halves.

On the training half we fit a T-learner: separate regression models μ^0\hat{\mu}_{0} and μ^1\hat{\mu}_{1} on the two arms. We estimated individual treatment effects in the training set as μ^1​(x)−yobs\hat{\mu}_{1}(x)-y_{\text{obs}} for controls and yobs−μ^0​(x)y_{\text{obs}}-\hat{\mu}_{0}(x) for the treated. We fit a depth-three regression tree to those individual effects, again in the training set, using all ten features, with leaves constrained to hold at least a hundredth of the sample. The depth constraint is just for legibility in this example; the method works with arbitrarily deep trees and offers a disciplined pruning strategy. The leaf constraint ensures the sample size is large enough to run the associated tests.

We applied the interwoven hierarchy of §3 to the resulting tree, with α=0.05,\alpha=0.05, stake vi=0.5v_{i}=0.5 at every node, equal weights between siblings, and threshold δ=0\delta=0 throughout. Directions were chosen on the training half, as in §4. All tests used the evaluation half. Each node’s hypothesis is tested by a one-sided Welch tt test on the relevant contrast—the difference of arm means for an effect hypothesis, and the difference-in-differences (y¯TR−y¯CR)−(y¯TL−y¯CL)(\bar{y}^{R}_{T}-\bar{y}^{R}_{C})-(\bar{y}^{L}_{T}-\bar{y}^{L}_{C}) for a heterogeneity one—with unpooled variances and Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The bounds of §6 come from inverting those same tests. Any test of the same contrasts at the desired level would serve.

Figure 2 shows the tree as fit on the training set. It correctly identified x2x_{2} as the most important predictor of effect heterogeneity, but detected x3x_{3} as an effect moderator only on the x2=0x_{2}=0 branch. On the x2=1x_{2}=1 branch, we found spurious heterogeneity with respect to x9.x_{9}.

Nodes and arrows can be solid or dashed, indicating whether we rejected the corresponding hypothesis with the specified FWER. From the top: the overall average treatment effect was positive (s.s.); the treatment effect among x2=1x_{2}=1 was higher than for x2=0x_{2}=0 (s.s.); among people having x2=0,x_{2}=0, the treatment effect was higher for people having x3=1x_{3}=1 than for x3=0x_{3}=0 (s.s.); the average treatment effect among people having x2=0,x3=0x_{2}=0,\,x_{3}=0 was negative (s.s.), but positive for x2=0,x3=1x_{2}=0,\,x_{3}=1 (s.s.), and so forth. The spurious heterogeneity with respect to x9x_{9} was not statistically significant. There are no Type-I errors shown in Figure 2, but we failed to identify heterogeneity with respect to x3x_{3} among the x2=1x_{2}=1 subpopulation.

Figure 3 shows the level at which each hypothesis is tested, the p-value, and for retained hypotheses, the “consolation prize” confidence bound. The figure shows, for example, that even though we cannot prove the treatment is beneficial for the x2=0,x_{2}=0, x3=1,x_{3}=1, x6>1.38x_{6}>1.38 group, we can bound how harmful it might be.

These insights go well beyond reporting overall average treatment effects. The casual observer may have drawn these same insights from a decision tree, but without any statistical guarantees. The testing procedure of §5 separates the reliable from the spurious.

7.2 Familywise error rate

The remaining studies compare five procedures on the same interwoven hierarchy: plain Bonferroni, which tests every hypothesis in the family at α/m\alpha/m; hierarchical Bonferroni, which halves the level at each depth; the fixed hierarchy procedure (v≡1v\equiv 1); the trickle down procedure with stake v≡1/2v\equiv 1/2; and a non-adaptive variant of the last, also at v≡1/2,v\equiv 1/2, forgoing direction selection entirely (every hypothesis is two-sided). Only the last procedure ignores the selected directions; the other four use them. Throughout, α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and n=4000.n=4000.

Table 2 shows the simulated familywise error rate for each procedure, the number of simulations where at least one true hypothesis was rejected. Under the global null, every procedure controls the familywise error rate, on a fixed partition and through a fitted tree alike. The worst cell is the fixed hierarchy procedure at 0.05080.0508 (s.e. 0.00350.0035). Plain Bonferroni is the most conservative, markedly so through a fitted tree.

Trickle down and hierarchical Bonferroni agree exactly, an artifact of the definition of familywise error rate. At v≡1/2v\equiv 1/2 with equal sibling weights the trickle down allocation is the halve-at-each-depth allocation, so recycling is the only thing separating the two procedures. Rejection triggers recycling, and under the global null a rejection is already a familywise error, so no amount of it can change whether one occurred.

The fitted-tree column shows no FWER inflation despite using an estimated partition. We measure both columns on the same populations, so the comparison between them is paired. Every paired difference is within noise except plain Bonferroni’s, which falls by 0.01030.0103 (s.e. 0.00420.0042) through the fitted tree. The direction is conservative, so the control claim holds.

7.3 Statistical power

The last section showed all procedures control the FWER at the specified level. This section investigates statistical power: how many true claims we certify, as a function of effect size. We scale two effect configurations by a factor to show how the procedure works on small and large effect sizes.

The first configuration is the running example of §7.1: the treatment helps on average and helps three quarters of the population, but harms the remaining quarter, so the average is misleading. The second is the same configuration with that quarter helped as well, so every effect points the same way. Table 3 displays the results.

The non-adaptive variant forgoes direction selection in both families: every hypothesis of both kinds is two-sided. Without a defensible strategy for selecting the direction of a one-sided test, the two-sided test is reasonable, but an increase in power is possible by using the training set to select the direction. At small effect sizes, where the adaptive strategy is more likely to choose the wrong side, it still certifies more true effects than the two-sided variant. Moreover, rejecting a two-sided hypothesis does not indicate on which side the truth lies and can lead to Type III errors. Table 3 credits both procedures for reaching a node, so it understates the difference.

Plain Bonferroni does surprisingly well, but this reveals a limitation of this evaluation strategy. Bonferroni gives less weight than the other methods to hypotheses early in the hierarchy, and more weight to the leaf hypotheses. There is only one root hypothesis, but many leaf hypotheses, so testing the latter at higher levels leads to more hypotheses rejected. This is an artifact of our shallow trees. In real examples, we may grow deeper trees with no risk of sacrificing reliability or power (except at the leaves) when using the multiplicity adjustments of §5. Plain Bonferroni is useless in deep trees whose hypothesis count doubles with each new level.

In our setting, hypotheses earlier in the hierarchy are more important; rejecting a leaf hypothesis is less valuable than rejecting the root hypothesis, but this is not reflected in Table 3. Table 4 shows how the procedures perform at each level. Fixed hierarchy has the highest power at the root, but plummets thereafter (as expected). Trickle down is almost as powerful at the root, but degrades more gracefully as we go deeper in the tree. Its advantage over Hierarchical Bonferroni mirrors Table 1.

8 Summary

Uplift models are often used to target a treatment where it will have the most benefit. The techniques of this paper can help interpret and validate such a strategy. Average treatment effects do not always tell the whole story and may mask a negative effect for some people. A responsible analyst will explore this possibility before administering the treatment to everyone.

Decision trees lead to interpretable descriptions of how the treatment effects vary across the population. Data splitting and multiplicity adjustments lead to honest estimates of treatment effects and trustworthy certification.

Table 4 showed Fixed Hierarchy had the best power for testing the root hypothesis, while plain Bonferroni had the best power for testing the leaf hypotheses. Analysts may use the Trickle Down stake, v,v, to tune the power available throughout the tree. A larger stake provides more power early in the hierarchy, while a smaller stake saves more power for later. The training data provide treatment effect estimates in each cell. It may be possible to use these estimates as guidance on how much power we need for each hypothesis. We could use this analysis to tune the stake for each hypothesis. We have not yet explored this.

Estimates and conclusions depend on the randomized split into training and evaluation sets. This may lead two analysts to draw different conclusions about treatment effects. We have not explored the stability of these conclusions under repeated splits; this variability is not captured in the significance levels or confidence bounds.

The hierarchy implies logical relations the procedure ignores. The average treatment effect in a node is a weighted average of the effects in the children, so a hypothesis about the parent can be false only if corresponding hypotheses about at least one child are false. Shaffer’s method (Shaffer, 1986) exploits such relations, but is not obviously applicable here because the directions of the tests in parent and child may differ.
